newsitem.title: IRAQ: China to sign $500 mln oil deal with Iraq - diplomat.
newsitem.headline: China to sign $500 mln oil deal with Iraq - diplomat.

text.p: The Chinese ambassador in Baghdad was quoted as saying on Monday that his country would soon sign a $500 million oil contract with Iraq to develop the Ahdad oilfield in the south.
A Chinese oil delegation headed by the chairman of the Chinese National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) Zhou Yong-Kang arrived in Baghdad on Sunday for discussions covering the billion-barrel Ahdab.
"The delegation will sign an agreement to develop Ahdab at a cost of $500 million," Chinese ambassador in Baghdad Sun Bi-Gan told the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya.
"The signing of this agreement will open new horizons for the consolidated and solidified relations betweean the two countries," Sun said.
A Chinese technical delegation was in Baghdad last week to prepare for the agreement. Iraq's National Assembly (parliament) last month gave its approval for the talks to go ahead.
The contract for Ahdab, discovered in 1979, will be implemented in 26 years, the paper said.
The official Iraqi News Agency said Zhou had his first meeting with Iraq's Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed on Monday. No details were given.
Oil officials say the Chinese are also interested in the development of the prized Halfaya field in the south.
Halfaya was discovered 20 years ago and is believed to hold commercial reserves of about five billion barrels. Iraq believes the field could produce some 250,000 barrels a day (bpd) at full capacity.

Iraq and Russia signed in March a $3.5 billion contract to develop seven to eight billion barrels of reserves in southern Iraq's Qurna oilfield, 500 km (300 miles) south of Baghdad. The deal will be implemented over 23 years.

United Nations trade sanctions imposed on Iraq for invading Kuwait in 1990 place a blanket ban on exports and investment in the country. The U.N. has allowed Iraq to pump $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for humanitarian purchases.
